title: Loops
oneLiner: Counting for loops and range, foreach and for-in, getting the index with enumerate or Index(), while and do-while, break and continue, off-by-one errors, zip and nested loops.
keyTakeaway: Prefer foreach (C#) or for-in (Python) when you just need the items: they can't run off the end. When you need positions, use half-open ranges (i < n, range(n)) so the count is end minus start, and check the empty, single-item and last-item cases by hand. break and continue only affect the innermost loop.
explanation:
A loop runs the same block of code repeatedly; each run is called an iteration. Loops are how a program processes every item in a list, retries until something succeeds, or counts through a range of numbers. They're also where most running time goes, so understanding how many times a loop runs is the first step towards Big O analysis.

There are two kinds. A for loop is for when you know what you're walking through: the numbers 0 to 9, or every item in a list. C# has a counting for loop with three parts (start, condition, step) and a foreach loop over a collection. Python's for always walks through a sequence; for counting you give it range(...), which produces the numbers. A while loop is for when you don't know in advance how many iterations it will take: it keeps going as long as a condition stays true.

Inside any loop, continue skips to the next iteration and break leaves the loop early. The most common loop bug is the off-by-one error, running one time too many or too few, usually from mixing up < with <= or forgetting that indexes stop at length minus 1.
